text:
ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on the newline token right after "assistant" (or similar paragraph-break positions) at the very start of a response, just before the model begins its reply, especially one that will open with a refusal ("I cannot provide…") or a persona/greeting. The negative pole fires on mid-word fragment tokens that begin or continue an acronym, code, or identifier (ISS-UED, HTML_AJAX, DQ-311, BW-430118), where the next token is a forced completion of the same word. So positive means a clean response boundary with an open, unconstrained start, while negative means being inside an unfinished token sequence where the continuation is predetermined.

LABEL: Fires at the newline that begins an assistant reply (often a refusal opener); goes negative on partial acronym/ID fragments mid-token where the next piece is forced.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on a single digit token that begins or sits inside a multi-digit number (IDs, dates, ports, card endings, times) where more digits or a unit (Oct, pm) are expected to follow. The negative pole fires at structural boundary tokens where the assistant's turn shifts into a new mode: "<tool_call>", the newline inside empty "<think>", or the first token of the reply, where what comes next is a word or function name rather than a digit. So the neuron separates "a numeric/identifier string is mid-formation" from "a formatting/turn-structure transition is occurring."

LABEL: Fires positive on a lone leading digit inside an ID, date, or number; negative on assistant-turn structural tokens like <tool_call> and the empty think newline.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole mostly fires on the newline/boundary token right before a `<tool_call>` block starts (or between consecutive tool calls), i.e. the point where the model is about to emit a function-call opening, with a few stray positives on commas, "from", and similar function-like tokens. The negative pole fires on mid-phrase tokens inside content being written or restated (a duplicated charge/refund reason, names like "Mel"/"Gabba", "of the", "Chicken Run") and on the newline preceding a plain-text reply, where the next token is ordinary prose or entity continuation rather than a tool call. So it appears to track whether the next thing is a structured tool-call opening (positive) versus continuing natural-language or content-like text (negative).

LABEL: Positive at the newline/boundary where a `<tool_call>` is about to begin; negative mid-phrase in prose, quoted reasons,

ANALYSIS: The strongly negative pole fires at the first token of an assistant reply (or the "assistant" role token) where the model is about to begin a refusal ("I cannot provide..."), so it marks the decision point of refusing a harmful request. The positive pole fires on mid-sentence function words (e.g., "else", "you", "if", "would") in a conditional or hypothetical position, such as offering or suggesting help ("Would you be open to...", "If you're feeling overwhelmed"), and generally continuing a sentence rather than stopping. Together it seems to track a compliance/refusal axis: negative = commit to refusing, positive = softly offering, continuing, or leaving a conditional/invitational frame open.

LABEL: Strongly negative at the start of an assistant's refusal ("I cannot..."); positive on mid-sentence conditional or invitational words ("if you", "would you", "no one else") off

ANALYSIS: Most strongly active tokens are mid-word fragments of rare proper names or invented words (Te|odor, Tid|ewater, Schn|ellenberger, Ven|k|ataraghavan, Perp|ignan, Bougez-B|ou|gez), where the next token completes an unusual multi-token name. Positive and negative poles seem to split on which specific fragment continuation is being predicted, so the neuron acts as a signed "this is an incomplete rare-name/word piece, predict its specific completion" feature. The negative pole also fires on structural newline tokens between consecutive tool calls (</tool_call>⏎<tool_call>), another predictable-continuation boundary.

LABEL: Fires on mid-word fragments of rare or unfamiliar names, positive or negative depending on the expected completion, and also on newline boundaries between consecutive tool calls.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on tokens inside a word or name that sit near the "net/nat/ne" letter cluster: positive on word-pieces like "networking", "JAN-ET", "Végét-ari-enne", "Niacin", and strongly negative on "Nen-ets", "nets", "Nep-al", "Nune-z", "Duch-enne". Its sign appears to split on which continuation is expected or what the token's phonetic form is, with ambiguity peaking at "ets" in rare proper names such as Nenets. Overall it handles mid-word subword fragments, especially "net/ne/ni"-like pieces, where the model must predict the rest of a rare name or word.

LABEL: Fires on subword fragments within rare words and names, especially "net/ne/ni" pieces: positive for networking/JANET-style tokens, strongly negative for "-ets" as in Nenets.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on tokens in mid-phrase or mid-structure positions where the next token is a fairly open continuation (a number, a noun, a modifier after "Use", "any", "how many"). The positive pole is dominated by list-item continuations and quantifier/determiner slots like "Using« different»", "Do you have« any»", and the negative pole by determiners and pronouns ("the", "their"), word-fragment tokens, and punctuation in narrative or structured text like "(retry)". It seems to encode a prediction-type distinction: positive when the next token is a content word or number from a broad set, negative when the next token is strongly constrained by the preceding word (a word completion, or a noun after "the/their").

LABEL: Splits tokens by predicted continuation: positive on slots before open content words, numbers, or quantifiers; negative on word fragments, determiners, and parentheses where the next token is high

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on mid-phrase tokens inside multi-token names, compounds, and technical terms where the word is clearly unfinished or a continuation is strongly expected (e.g. "Golden« Gate»", "mer«itor»ious", "Le«itz»", "sax»ophone", "tax« code»"). The negative pole fires on structural boundary tokens (the empty "</think>" slot, paragraph-break newlines, numeral fragments, "cable") where the next token is a fresh start or an almost deterministic formatting continuation. So the neuron roughly separates "inside an entity or term, predicting its specific completion" from "at a clause or turn boundary, or a digit-completion slot".

LABEL: Positive on mid-word or mid-name fragments needing a specific completion; negative on structural boundaries (</think>, paragraph breaks) and digit fragments of years.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on word-fragment or second-position tokens that complete a compound/field-name key (member_since, created, refunds, bed-rooms, Tid-ewater, Ref-inement), mostly in structured tool-call/record contexts where a key or identifier is just finishing. The negative pole fires on the head noun of a noun phrase (support, dust, fee, event, profile, calendar) whose referent was already introduced, i.e. a token that names a previously mentioned or generic entity rather than completing a new compound. So the neuron seems to separate tokens that complete a novel label or identifier (positive) from tokens that refer back to an already established concept (negative).

LABEL: Positive on tokens completing a newly formed compound name or field key (member_since, created, refunds); negative on head nouns re-referencing an already-introduced concept.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires strongly (up to +67) on structural/formatting tokens inside agentic tool-call transcripts and structured records: closing tags, parameter delimiters, newlines, digits and punctuation within IDs, dates, and code, where the next token is highly predictable boilerplate. The negative pole is weak (about -2 to -6) and appears on tokens in ordinary chat prose, especially "Would you «like»", "hosted «by»", and the start of assistant turns, where the next token is open-ended or a conversational continuation. So the neuron separates rigid, template-driven, machine-formatted continuation (strongly positive) from free-form natural-language continuation (slightly negative).

LABEL: Fires hugely on delimiter/formatting/ID tokens in tool-call and structured-record text with predictable continuations; slightly negative on open-ended conversational prose tokens like "

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at the start of the assistant's turn or a new tool call/response, where the model is about to begin its own output (after `<|im_start|>assistant`, `<tool_call>`, `<function`), including the opening quote or first-person "I" that begins a new speaker's utterance. The negative pole fires at the first token of a new sentence or paragraph in human-written prose (often a first-person "I", "One", "You"), and in the system prompt on "in" at the point where the style instruction is given. Both poles sit at a boundary where a new segment or voice begins, with the sign separating agentic or assistant-output starts (positive) from human or style-framing starts (negative).

LABEL: Marks segment-start boundaries: positive when the assistant or a tool call begins its own output, negative at sentence-initial first-person words in human prose and system style instructions.

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire mostly on mid-word tokens, where the model is partway through a word or name and the next piece is still to come. The positive pole is dominated by "light/shine/radiate" word-starts (Radi-, shine, gleaming, glitter-, luminos-, spectacles, radiation), with a scattering of name fragments such as "Stephen/Gould" and "Gab-ba". The negative pole is mostly name or compound fragments (Ekb-org, Afanas-iev, Chamb-ord, Wren-field, Samarit-ans, flick-ering) that predict a specific suffix completion.

LABEL: Fires on mid-word subword fragments, positive for light/shining-related word pieces (radi-, gleam-, shine) and negative for proper-name or compound fragments awaiting a suffix.

ANALYSIS: Positive activations fire on tokens in the middle of a compound or camelCase identifier or acronym, where the preceding token is a fragment that must be followed by a continuation (e.g. "v|Card", "$software|Name", "Me|SH", "#Stay|Warm"). Positive also hits newline or delimiter tokens inside structured tool calls. Negative activations fire on ordinary prose function/continuation words or name fragments (in, to, with, "-", "**", "Call|um", "Dore|en"), where the next token is a predictable ordinary word or a name completion.

LABEL: Positive on mid-token fragments of camelCase/hashtag/acronym identifiers needing continuation; negative on ordinary prose connectors, bullets, and split-name fragments.

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on mid-word sub-token fragments inside rare or multi-token words and names, where the model is partway through spelling out a word. The positive pole is dominated by a few specific continuations (obl-ivious, Samar-it-ans, Newport P-agn-ell, ob-vious, ol-ive), mostly where the next piece is highly predictable. The negative pole fires on unusual or fabricated names (V-ell-entine, vel-mor-ite, Pfa-el-zer, Orns-by), where the continuation is less certain.

LABEL: Mid-word token fragments in rare or multi-token words and names; positive when the completion is well-known or predictable, negative for obscure, invented names.

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire mostly on mid-word fragment tokens or word-boundary tokens, where the model must work out what the sequence is becoming. At the positive pole the token tends to complete or sit inside a known compound, name, or template ("Burkin", "Scene", "timeline", "Here is a piece of text:"), so the next step is highly predictable. At the negative pole the token is typically a split inside a rarer or unfamiliar proper noun or word ("Kaluga", "Meckiff", "Saw|to|oth"), where the continuation is less constrained and requires reconstructing the whole word.

LABEL: Positive on tokens whose continuation is a familiar, predictable compound or template; negative on mid-word pieces of rare proper nouns or words whose completion is uncertain.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at token positions where the model is mid-structure and must decide how to continue: positive on tokens that open or sit inside a construct (tool-call syntax, generics, a "(" or "—", digits within a number), where the next token is tightly constrained or the clause is still unfinished. Negative values mostly fall on sentence-final or unit-final tokens (periods, closing tags, closing quotes) where a thought or segment is complete and a boundary or new turn follows. So it roughly tracks "continuation of an unfinished unit" versus "completion and boundary," with the poles reading as opposite signs of the same axis.

LABEL: Positive on tokens inside unfinished constructs (open syntax, mid-number, mid-phrase); negative on tokens that complete a sentence or unit (periods, closing tags/quotes), marking boundaries.

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on the first or middle sub-word fragment of a word or name that has just been split into pieces, mostly capitalized proper nouns and list-item openers. Positive activations favor rare, invented-sounding names and odd fragments (Ushk-ari, Fenn-ick, Wren-field) where the continuation is unpredictable. Negative activations favor common, concrete, familiar words and well-known names (L'Oréal, Zinc, Food, Chanel, Vinci), where the identity is already strongly implied.

LABEL: Fires on word-fragment tokens inside split names; positive when the word is novel or obscure and unpredictable, negative when it is a familiar, recognizable word or name.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole mostly fires at the structural boundary where an assistant turn begins, especially the closing "</think>" token of an empty think block right before the reply starts, and occasionally at the first function word of a response that opens a new section or list. The negative pole fires on mid-sentence tokens that project forward to a specific continuation, such as "flag" (in "flag this conversation"), "In [this/many/some] case", and "look into/at", where the next token is strongly constrained. Overall it separates "about to begin an open-ended assistant response" from "mid-phrase with a highly predictable next word."

LABEL: Positive at response-start boundaries (end of empty think block, new section openers); negative mid-phrase where the next word is predictable, e.g. "flag this", "In this case", "look into".

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on tokens where the next word is highly predictable from a fixed phrase or formula ("Salt and pepper to taste", "like, share and subscribe", "Reduce, re-use, and recycle", "bow deeply", "Ad-supported"), often a conjunction, article or preposition awaiting a stereotyped completion. The negative pole fires on tokens where the continuation is more open or about to be a hyphenated/compound or modifier slot ("well-organized", "his and her", "wrap around", "costly mistakes", "as" in "such as"), where many different continuations are possible. So the neuron seems to track how strongly the current token commits the model to a specific, formulaic next token versus leaving it open.

LABEL: Positive on tokens mid-way through stock phrases whose next word is nearly fixed (e.g. "salt and pepper"); negative on tokens leading into open-

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires inside narrative or descriptive prose, on tokens that set up a relative or subordinate clause or end a sentence, where the next word is likely a pronoun (he/she/they) or a new narrative sentence. The negative pole fires in assistant-style structure: the empty `</think>` token, a comma after "In the United States," or "If it doesn't exist," or the "Let me…" planning and tool-call lines. In short, it tracks the register: story/essay continuation (positive) versus structured assistant, safety, or reasoning scaffolding (negative).

LABEL: Positive at clause/sentence junctures in narrative prose predicting a pronoun subject; strongly negative at assistant scaffolding like empty think-close, crisis-hotline commas, and planning or tool-call transitions.

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on structural/formatting boundary tokens (newlines, whitespace indentation, tag delimiters, operators) at points where the next token is highly predictable or begins a new unit, such as after assistant turn starts, `<think>` closings, or code operators. Positive activations mostly sit on separator/delimiter tokens that begin a tool call or response, and on connector symbols like "-" in arithmetic. Negative activations sit on the first token of a new content element (e.g. `$$`, ` json`, identifier fragments, newline in prose/code blocks) where content or formatting is about to be chosen.

LABEL: Fires on formatting and delimiter tokens (newlines, turn/tool-call tags, operators) at structural boundaries; sign flips between the boundary itself (positive) and content-opening tokens such as math, code, and prose starts (negative).

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires strongly on the first token of an assistant reply that opens with an affirmation ("Certainly", "Sure", "Of course!", "Yes"), at the point where the model has agreed and is about to start the actual content; a few cases are mid-sentence "as well"/"cost"/"consequences" where a clause is complete and elaboration is about to follow. The negative pole is weak and fires on tokens inside ongoing, stylized or deliberative discourse (archaic "thou" roleplay, "Let me check/reconsider", "consider") where the model is stalling or mid-clause, not yet delivering the answer.

LABEL: Fires on the affirmative acknowledgment token opening an assistant reply ("Certainly!", "Sure", "Of course!"), just before content starts; weakly negative on mid-clause stalling or roleplay tokens.

ANALYSIS: The strong positive pole fires on tokens that are the letter "D" or begin a "Dan-/Dak-/Dop-" word (Danish, Denmark, D-Biotin, dopamine, Dakota, d1-Alpha), i.e. a token that starts with or is the letter D. The weak negative pole is scattered across mid-word fragments and other letters (C, K, N, plant, snack, .yaml, orbit), with no clear D-association. So it acts mainly as a "this token is D / D-initial" detector, with negative values being weak, diffuse non-D word-piece activity.

LABEL: Detects tokens that are or begin with the letter "D" (Danish, D-Biotin, dopamine, Dakota); weakly negative on unrelated word fragments and other letters.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at structural boundary tokens in agentic/tool-use chat transcripts: the assistant-turn start, the blank line after an empty think block, newlines before tool calls or after user headers, and identifier digits like account/approval numbers. The negative pole fires mid-word or mid-phrase in creative-writing, romance, list-style or safety-refusal text, on name fragments and continuation tokens such as "Lovel|ace", "Crisis| Text", and "Mel|anie". So it separates tool/agent workflow structure and ID tokens (positive) from flowing prose and multi-token names or phrases (negative).

LABEL: Positive at turn/format boundary tokens and ID digits in agentic tool-use transcripts; negative inside multi-token names and phrases in creative or conversational prose.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on a verb at the position right after a subject (or modal) and predicts what comes next. The positive pole is perception/inspection verbs (review, see, notice, investigate, detect, find) that take an object to be examined, often a third party that "will review this." The negative pole is transfer/communication/assistance verbs (provide, tell, suggest, help, submit, throw, encourage, agree) that hand something to a recipient, especially after "I can".

LABEL: Verb slot after a subject/modal: positive for examine/perceive verbs (review, see, notice), negative for give/tell/provide/help verbs that direct something toward a recipient.

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire at mid-sentence points where the next token is a syntactic continuation, such as "to", a comma, "which", or a period after a clause or noun phrase. The positive pole is mostly expository or advice text where a purpose, benefit or consequence clause comes next ("to enhance...", ", which allows..."). The negative pole is mostly assistant replies that begin or elaborate on a subject already in the user's prompt, or that restate a just-named feature (sofa speaker "system", "halo", "options"), and it is strongest at the start of a response and when the model echoes or confirms something already stated.

LABEL: Predicts what follows a clause: positive when a new purpose/benefit clause is being introduced ("to", "which", comma); negative when echoing or elaborating entities from the prompt or earlier turns.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at tokens in text about the cost, price, or payment of products and services, with negative activation on the payment side (people paying for or not paying for content, "normally cost money", paywalls, funding, premium tiers) and positive on the provider side (free trials, "we offer", transparent prices, no contracts, rental fees). It marks mid-phrase tokens (connectives, "to", "offer") where the text is working toward a statement about money, pricing, or access terms, in the way a predictive unit anticipating "pay/free/cost/price" would. The strongest signal is the negative pole on "willingness to pay" contexts.

LABEL: Tracks pricing/payment/free-vs-paid framing: strongly negative where consumers pay or avoid paying for content, positive where providers advertise free trials, offers, or transparent pricing.

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire inside text about publications, such as journals, articles, studies, books and publishers, and on small function tokens (of, the, and, a, year digits) where the next word is expected to name or describe a publication or its source. The sign appears to track whether the model is predicting a generic publication-related continuation (positive) versus a specific bibliographic or study-citation detail like a named study, date digit, or author-attributed article (negative). So it is a publication-context predictor that splits on generic versus specific/cited referent.

LABEL: Fires on function words and punctuation in publishing/journal/article contexts, positive when generic publication talk is expected, negative when a specific cited study, article, or date follows.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on sentence- or clause-closing punctuation (periods, commas, newlines, closing parens) and similar boundary tokens, where a complete unit has just ended and a new one begins. The negative pole fires on tokens in the middle of a unit that is still unfinished or tightly bound to what follows: the last word of a header or identifier before a closing mark, and words expecting a continuation (“to”, “Order ID”, “text HOME”, “Name” in variable names). So it separates "a unit is complete, move on" from "inside a name/term/phrase that must continue or be closed".

LABEL: Positive on clause/sentence-ending punctuation marking a completed unit; negative on mid-phrase or mid-identifier tokens (headers, variable names, "to", "HOME") that need continuation.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on tokens that complete a unit and set up a predictable next token: a unit noun after a quantity ("seconds", "minutes", "pm"), a newline before the next numbered list item ("2."), and the head noun of a fixed phrase ("Race", "Amendment"). The negative pole fires on tokens where the continuation is open or a turn or structure boundary must be handled: newlines after <|im_end|>, closing tags, mid-phrase articles and affixes ("a", "the", "pre", "'"), and the start of a new user turn. So the neuron separates "structure-completing, next-item-predictable" positions (positive) from "turn-boundary or mid-phrase, open-continuation" positions (negative).

LABEL: Positive on tokens completing a quantity, list item or fixed phrase before an expected numbered continuation; negative on chat-turn boundary newlines,

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at structural boundary tokens where the assistant's response is about to begin or a new structured block starts (after `</think>`, before `<tool_call>`, at `<|im_start|>assistant`, table header cells), and especially on the first token of a refusal. The negative pole fires on a mid-sentence or mid-list token (a continuation word, colon, newline) in ordinary helpful-assistant prose. Both poles seem to track a "what kind of response comes next" decision: a firm, formulaic mode (refusal, tool call, table) is boosted, while open-ended generic elaboration is suppressed.

LABEL: Positive at response/block-start boundary tokens (refusal openings, tool calls, table headers); negative on mid-sentence continuation tokens in free-form helpful prose.

ANALYSIS: The strong positive activations fall on a token (often a mid-phrase adjective, conjunction, or word-piece) where the next token is highly predictable and begins with "v" — "well"→ventilated, "bullet-proof"→vest, "serious"→violation, "chicken or"→vegetable, "cider"→vinegar, "operating system"→verifies. The neuron seems to boost the "v" initial prediction (verify, violation, vegetable, vinegar, vapor, voice, volume). The negative pole is tiny in magnitude (about -2) and appears to be diffuse near-zero noise with no clear pattern, so this is effectively a one-sided neuron.

LABEL: Fires strongly when the next token should start with "v" (violation, vegetable, ventilated, verify, vinegar, vest); negative pole is weak, diffuse noise.

ANALYSIS: Activations are huge in magnitude and fire at structural/boundary tokens (end of turn markers, `<think>`, closing brackets, line breaks, punctuation, list numerals) inside code and formatted text. The positive pole fires on these boundary tokens in mixed-case chat/PowerShell/Java contexts, while the negative pole fires (much more strongly) on the same kinds of tokens in contexts where the text is entirely lowercased, e.g. lowercased C#/Java code, numbered lists, and prose. It looks like a case-/text-normalization-sensitive "structural token" detector: sign flips depending on whether the surrounding text is in normal casing or has been lowercased.

LABEL: Fires on structural boundary tokens (punctuation, newlines, turn markers, list numbers), positive in normally-cased text, strongly negative when the surrounding text is all lowercased.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on function tokens (commas in lists, "be", "as", "the", "are", "of") that sit right before a predictable continuation, and goes negative strongly on "make/making/become/makes" and some list commas where a verb-of-creation or a specific noun phrase follows. The two poles look like opposite predictions for the upcoming token: positive favors continuations like "amount", "be", "recyclable", "limit", list items, while negative favors continuations like "it/them/you" after make, or a particular list item. It is therefore tied to syntactic slot prediction (what grammatical category comes next) rather than to topic.

LABEL: Predicts next-token slot at function words: positive before quantity/"be"/list-continuation nouns, negative on "make/become" verbs and some list commas awaiting an object or complement.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on achievement/flourishing words (especially "successful", "success", "competitive", "effective", "thrive"), often right after "a/to be", and on commas after infinitive purpose clauses ("To test X,"). The negative pole fires on modal/obligation and requirement words ("must", "need", "require", "can", "to", "that") where the next token is a predicate or condition for something, with a lean toward stated constraints or prerequisites. Both poles concern the goal/requirement frame, where positive marks the desired outcome being named and negative marks the necessity or condition word that leads up to it.

LABEL: Positive on desired-outcome words like "successful" or "thrive" (and commas after goal clauses); negative on requirement/modal words like "must", "need", "require" setting conditions.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on tokens that open a new bracketed or emphasized span in expository text: an opening parenthesis, bold markers, quotes, or a paragraph break after an introduced named entity or list item. The negative pole fires on boundaries that start the assistant's own first-person response or voice: after `</think>`, after a closing quote before narration like "I turn…", or at a comma or dash after a refusal or hedge ("However,"). So the neuron appears to separate "start of an aside, label, or named item in third-person description" (positive) from "start of the assistant's own speech or stance" (negative).

LABEL: Token right at a structural boundary: positive when opening an aside/bold/parenthetical about a named item; negative when starting the assistant's own first-person reply or narration.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at word-internal or mid-name subword tokens, where the current fragment is the middle or end of a proper noun or rare word and the model must decide how the word continues or closes. Positive activations come mainly on tokens ending a name (ashBY, CAMH, Banksy, Timbuktu) or following a "tim"-like start; negative activations come on fragments beginning with g/gr/gri ("grim", "Briggs", "Grigori", "Grin", "grill") or other strongly predicted continuations. So it seems to track whether a split word/name fragment is a completed ending versus an unfinished g-/gr- start expecting more letters.

LABEL: Mid-word subword fragments of names/rare words: positive on tokens completing a name (-by, -H, -y), negative on g/gr-initial fragments (grim, Grigori, Briggs, grill) that expect continuation.

ANALYSIS: At the positive pole, the neuron fires on a sentence-ending period or comma right after the assistant's (or a speaker's) opening or transitional sentence, where the next token is "I" beginning a first-person statement (e.g. "Thank you, Margaret. I can see…", "I know the definition of grief… I have never lost. I know…"). At the negative pole, it fires strongly on structural boundary tokens (newlines after tool responses, end-of-turn markers, conjunctions mid-user-request) where the next token is a turn boundary, a user query, or a non-"I" continuation. Overall it appears to predict whether the upcoming token is the first-person pronoun "I" (positive) versus a role/turn/structure token or other continuation (negative).

LABEL: Predicts whether the next token is a first-person "I" starting a sentence (positive) versus a turn-boundary, newline, or non-"

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on the middle or end of rare proper-name fragments (Gurpur, Minogue, Birkinshaw, Vistria, Meroșin), mostly inside author lists in citations, where the next token is a name continuation or a comma. The negative pole fires strongly on "calcium"/"Calc-ium"/"Ca"/"lime"/"Lime" (and mildly "mineral"), i.e. tokens in the Ca-/Lim-/Cal- family used as chemistry or company words. Both poles seem to track a word-piece identity question, where the neuron separates mid-name fragments from a specific cluster of "calcium/lime/mineral" tokens.

LABEL: Positive on mid-word fragments of rare surnames (esp. citation author lists); strongly negative on "calcium"/"lime" (Ca/Lim/Cal) tokens, weakly

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on function words, punctuation, and mid-phrase tokens (to, the, a, commas, newlines, name fragments) where the next token is highly open-ended or a continuation is syntactically required. It has no consistent topic or token identity at either pole, and the same tokens (e.g., "to", "the", newline after im_end) appear on both sides, so the sign seems to reflect a hidden direction in how the prediction is being set up. The positive pole skews toward list/instructional or expository contexts, while the negative pole skews toward refusals, narrative, and safety-adjacent or ethically loaded contexts.

LABEL: Fires on syntactic glue tokens (to, the, a, commas, newlines) awaiting an open continuation; sign shifts between neutral expository/instructional text (positive) and refusal/narrative/ethical contexts (negative).

ANALYSIS: The neuron sits at structural or boundary positions (whitespace indentation, newlines, role tokens like <|im_start|>, list numerals, punctuation) and fires at weakly positive levels on them, with two huge outliers at an indent token inside test code. The strong positive cases (22.2, and 5-6 at "suppress"/"empathy") and the strong negative ones ("willing to", "democracy.") look like sparse, high-magnitude outliers where the model is committing to a specific next-token continuation, with sign flipping between near-opposite contexts. Overall it behaves as a low-activation structural-delimiter detector that occasionally spikes in either direction at tokens that set up a decisive next step.

LABEL: Fires weakly on structural delimiters (newlines, role tokens, indents, list numbers); rare large spikes in either direction at tokens that strongly constrain the next token.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at the point where the model is about to affirm or verify something against evidence it has just retrieved (tool results, records, logs) — e.g. "Payment history [confirmed]", "Let me check the logs [to] confirm", "[can] confirm", and the closing of tool responses before the assistant reports findings. The negative pole fires where the model is instructed or about to supply supporting material (use examples/sources "to" support claims, "provide examples/reasons"), i.e. a pending demand for illustrative support rather than a check against ground truth. Both poles mark positions predicting a verification/evidence-related continuation, with positive = confirming/verifying grounded facts and negative = providing or requesting supporting examples.

LABEL: Predicts a verification/confirmation word next (positive: confirming against retrieved records or tool output) versus supplying supporting examples or sources (negative: "use examples

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at tokens where the assistant is about to wrap up or pivot in careful, self-monitoring, hedging or verification-style text (e.g., "Everything looks good", "it's possible", "you might be thinking"), and at structural boundaries like turn-ending newlines and markdown headers. The negative pole fires at similar structural/transition tokens in terse, confident, mechanical contexts (the newline after a tool call ending, numbered action lists, and quick factual answers in plain, non-reasoning style). So it appears to track whether the model is in a deliberative, uncertainty-aware, self-checking mode (positive) versus a straightforward, executing, confident-output mode (negative), mostly read off at boundary or transition tokens.

LABEL: At turn/section boundaries and hedge tokens, fires positive in deliberative, self-checking, uncertainty-hedging text and

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at tokens that sit mid-word or mid-phrase, where the next token is a strongly constrained continuation of an already-started unit. Positive activations mostly land on the final or closing piece of multi-token names, acronyms, and numbers (rPPG, ECG, TDEE, 1.725), where the unit is complete or nearly so. The much stronger negative activations land on word fragments, or on a word that opens a fixed phrase, and these are followed by a predictable specific continuation (Phy-isc-s, Jul/Aug in dates, "Suppose", mala, immersion, counter-example).

LABEL: Tracks position within multi-token units: weakly positive at the end of completed acronyms and names, strongly negative on fragments and phrase-openers whose next token is highly predictable.

ANALYSIS: Positive activations fire on tokens in the middle of a topic-specific phrase or narrative whose concept is already established, such as "rewind time", "immobilization", or "teleport", especially pronouns and function words (she, her, to) that continue it. Negative activations fire on the key token of a distinctive set phrase or proper name, such as "go private", "Saint-Rémy", "van Gogh", or "Statutory Sick", where the token itself carries the specific content. So the neuron seems to separate tokens that carry on a recurring theme from tokens that complete a rigid, memorized collocation.

LABEL: Fires on continuation tokens and pronouns within an ongoing topical theme (time-rewind, immobilization); goes negative on tokens completing fixed collocations or names like "go private", "Saint-Rémy", "van Gogh".

ANALYSIS: Activations land on mid-phrase function words, subword fragments, and punctuation where the next token is a highly constrained continuation (e.g., "controlling→for", "none→of", "can→'t", "main→()"), but there is no clean split by token type, as the same kinds of tokens appear at both poles. The sign seems to track which kind of continuation is predicted: positive when the next token is a function word or phrase-completing piece after the current word, negative when it is a content word, a repeated or copied term, or a subject pronoun ("you") beginning a clause. Overall it looks like a next-token-prediction-structure neuron operating at word-internal and phrase-internal positions rather than a topic detector.

LABEL: Fires at mid-phrase tokens (function words, subword pieces, punctuation), with sign reflecting whether the predicted continuation is a function/phrase-completing word (positive) or a content, cop

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at boundary or completion points: ends of tool responses, sentence-final periods, closing brackets, and list/table delimiters, where a unit has just finished and a new segment (assistant turn, new item) begins. The negative pole fires mid-clause on function words and pronouns (his, a, to, they, she, or, of) at the start of a sentence or phrase where the continuation is still wide open and syntactically demanded. So the neuron seems to encode "structural unit closed, next token is a fresh start" versus "unit in progress, a continuation is required."

LABEL: Positive on closure points (sentence ends, tool-response ends, delimiters); negative on mid-phrase function words and pronouns that demand a continuation.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on tokens in the middle of a multi-token identifier, number, or name (digits inside IDs like HD-4«4»71, dates, name fragments, "port:« »8080"), where the next token is a tightly predictable continuation of an unfinished unit. The negative pole fires on tokens that complete a unit or mark a boundary, such as newlines before a tool call, ticket IDs followed by a space, or the start of a snake_case/handle segment, where the next token begins something new or is a structural delimiter.

LABEL: Positive on mid-token fragments of IDs, numbers, and names that are still unfinished; negative on boundary tokens (newlines, spaces, separators) where a structural unit just ended.

ANALYSIS: Positive activations concentrate at the start of an assistant turn, at the "assistant" token or the newline or think-closing token just before the reply begins, where the model is about to write a direct, natural-language answer to a user. They also fire at some mid-sentence words where a statement is being set up, such as "is" and "if". Negative activations occur where the model is about to emit a structured or tool-call output, as with "<tool_call>" and parameter tags, or at spots inside a fixed continuation or structured format.

LABEL: Fires at assistant-turn start when a prose reply to the user is coming; goes negative when a tool call or structured/formulaic continuation follows.

ANALYSIS: Positive activations fall mostly on mid-clause tokens (auxiliaries, prepositions, participles, commas) where the next token is open-ended and the sentence continues with a verb phrase or predicate. Negative activations fall on tokens that have just completed a unit and where the continuation is highly predictable or formulaic: "place", "next", "each", "previous", closing tags like ">" and "-" in structured tool outputs, and turn delimiters. So the neuron appears to track whether the model is mid-phrase awaiting an open continuation (positive) or at a spot where the following token is nearly determined by a fixed pattern (negative).

LABEL: Positive on mid-clause function words awaiting an open predicate; negative on tokens in fixed or repetitive patterns (next, each, previous, template closers, delimiters) where continuation is predictable.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at structural boundary tokens of chat turns, mostly <|im_end|>. The positive pole is the end of a complete assistant reply (a closing statement, with a tool-response turn or end of conversation as the expected next step) and the "user" role token carrying a tool_response. The negative pole is the end of an assistant turn that expects a follow-up user message with a conversational "Thank you/Can you..." request, plus the first user/assistant tokens of a new turn and newlines opening a reply.

LABEL: Chat-turn boundary tokens: positive when an assistant turn closes definitively or hands off to tool output, negative when the next turn is a conversational user follow-up or reply start.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on words right after "the" (or similar determiners) that refer to a contrasting counterpart or already-mentioned member of a set, mostly "other/others," also "previous," "first," "before," "rest." The model is tracking a noun-less anaphoric reference to "the one that isn't this one." The negative pole is weak and diffuse, showing up on words where the next token is more open-ended, such as "essential" (predicting "to"), "download," and "a Lady," with a mild negative on "other" in some contexts.

LABEL: Fires on "other/others/previous/first/rest" after "the," marking a contrasting counterpart referent; weakly negative on predicate adjectives like "essential" and verbs awaiting a complement.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires mostly on the newline right after "assistant" at the start of an assistant turn, where the model is about to begin its reply, usually a tool call or an "I'll look into…" opener; it also hits some mid-word or role-label tokens in dialogue. The negative pole fires on tokens that start a new sub-structure inside a turn, such as the "<" opening the next tool_call or parameter, the word "something" in a user's confession opener, and mid-phrase tokens in tool-response data. In both cases the neuron tracks structural boundary or turn-start positions, with positive meaning the assistant is about to begin acting and negative meaning a slot inside the current content is being filled or continued.

LABEL: Positive at the newline opening an assistant turn (about to reply or call a tool); negative at structure-opening tokens inside content, like "<" of the next tool call or parameter.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on the "\n\n" token right after an empty think block, immediately before a response that begins "I cannot provide...", plus scattered boundary or punctuation tokens just before a first-person "I" sentence. The negative pole fires on tokens where "I" has just been, or is about to be, treated as a name or letter fragment (I.M. Pei, I-35W, "All I Want", "I"liad", Zane-is), plus list numerals and structural tokens. So the neuron seems to track whether an upcoming "I" is a first-person pronoun starting a statement (positive) or an "I" that is part of a name or title (negative).

LABEL: Predicts a sentence-initial first-person "I" (especially refusals "I cannot...") at the position before it; strongly negative where "I" is a name/title fragment or list numeral.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires strongly at structural joints in the assistant's turn — the "a" in "says a lot," paragraph breaks after empathetic openers, "isn't" in "There isn't a single right answer," end-of-turn tokens, and tool-call boundaries — mostly in emotionally weighty or tool-using replies. The negative pole is weak (about -1.2) and sits on similar boundary tokens (paragraph breaks, commas, digits, "I'll start by reading the file") in neutral, task-oriented or generic informational replies. So it's a one-sided magnitude signal marking a point where the assistant is about to deliver a supportive, hedged, or procedurally transitional continuation, strongest for heavy confessional contexts.

LABEL: Fires strongly at transition/boundary tokens in empathetic, guilt-laden confessional replies and tool-call handoffs; stays

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on mid-word fragments of rare proper names (surnames, place names, brand names) split into several subword tokens, usually the 2nd or 3rd piece where the word is still incomplete. The sign appears to depend on which fragment/continuation is predicted (e.g. "Hod|ges", "Reg|gis" positive vs "Reg|ent", "Wuebb|les", "Tre|uw" negative), so it is mainly a token-identity-dependent signal for unfinished rare-name pieces rather than a topic. It is weak in magnitude and also appears on a few ordinary word pieces such as "government".

LABEL: Fires on mid-word subword fragments of rare multi-token proper names, with sign varying by which fragment it is (e.g. "ges"/"gis" positive, "ent"/"les"/"ick" negative).

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on structural/formatting tokens inside a response that is already mid-stream in a list or heading: the colon or newline right after a numbered list item's title, or the bullet-like separators that introduce the item's explanatory body. The negative pole fires on the `<think>` token at the start of an assistant turn (especially before a refusal) and on closing/punctuation tokens that end an item or label in structured reports. Both poles mark a boundary-delimiting token where the model must decide what kind of content comes next, with positive predicting an elaborative explanation continuing a list and negative predicting a fresh start or terminal verdict/refusal.

LABEL: Fires on boundary tokens: positive at colons/newlines after list-item titles (elaboration follows), negative at assistant-turn-start `<think>` and item-closing tokens before refusals/verdicts.

ANALYSIS: The strongest positive activations fall on tokens that begin or sit inside a word or name where the identity is fixed but not yet completed, such as "me" in meow, "har" in harp, "puls" in pulsating, and "Mira", plus a few bare animal or country names like "cat" and "Egypt". The negative side shows the same kind of mid-word fragments, such as "Nep"(al), "Kar"(imi), "Lu"(anda), "Nap"(oleon), and digits within years. These are predominantly the same sort of token, but the neuron seems to separate them by which word is likely to complete next, with a strong cat/animal and Egypt/Mira lean on the positive side and freight/Nepal/1980s-style continuations on the negative side. This looks like a feature tied to predicting specific next-token continuations rather than to any topic.

LABEL: Fires on mid-word fragments and named-ent

ANALYSIS: Positive activations land mostly on abstract, relational or stative verbs and adverbs (share, reflect, located, intimately, represents, embodied) where the model is describing how something is connected, expressed or held in common. Negative activations land on concrete, action-oriented imperatives or verbs of manipulation and request (convince, flip, fix, sort, set, book, store), often right after "How do I / Can you / Could you", where a physical or agentive task is being requested. So the axis seems to run from describing a state or shared relationship (positive) to commanding or requesting an actual task or manipulation (negative).

LABEL: Distinguishes stative/relational verbs of sharing, reflecting and being located (positive) from agentive task-request verbs like fix, flip, sort, convince after "How do I/Can you" (negative).

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires at the first token of a new assistant clause or sentence (often "Now" after a tool response, "If" starting a refusal's redirect, or a comma or "that" introducing a clause), usually just before the model addresses "you" or states its next action. The negative pole is weak and falls on similar boundary tokens (such as "want", "Would", "tell", "if", or newline after a sentence) in empathetic, confidentiality-focused or hedging turns. The neuron appears to mark a clause-transition point where the model is committing to a direction, with a strong push when the continuation is a plain, directive statement and mild suppression when it is a soft or tentative one.

LABEL: Fires at clause/sentence-opening transition tokens right before the assistant states its next step or addresses "you" directly; weakly negative at similar soft, empathetic or tentative junctures.

ANALYSIS: Activations are hugely asymmetric: the negative pole reaches about -50 to -78 while the positive side tops out near +4, so the neuron is mainly a strong negative detector. It fires strongly negative at structural decision points where the assistant is starting or pivoting its reply, e.g. the "assistant" token after a harmful request (right before "I cannot…"), and the comma or period after "If you're interested in X," that turns a refusal into a redirect to safe topics. It also fires at the same kind of position in the customer-service refund transcripts (tool-call delimiters, "I understand… Margaret, and"), while the weak positive side is scattered across mid-word tokens, digits and ordinary role-boundary tokens in benign contexts.

LABEL: Strongly negative at assistant-turn onset and comma/period pivot tokens where the model commits to a refusal-or-redirect or scripted ag

ANALYSIS: Positive activations fall on structural boundary tokens where a new segment begins and the next token is likely a fresh start (e.g., "</think>" before the reply, newlines after turn ends, tool-call separators, paragraph breaks before dialogue). Negative activations fall on punctuation or function words (period, comma, "However,") where the next token is very likely a first-person pronoun "I" (or "Francis"/"what"), i.e. the sentence continues with a predictable subject. So the neuron seems tied to what comes next: confident prediction of "I" or a continuation word (negative) versus an open start of new content or turn (positive).

LABEL: Positive at structural/turn/paragraph boundaries opening new content; negative at clause-ending punctuation or connectives right before a predicted first-person "I" or similar continuation.

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on mid-word or mid-name tokens where the next token is a continuation of the same word or name, but the two poles seem to differ in how settled the continuation is. Positive cases are rare proper-name fragments (Gaga, Halvorsen, Tidewater, Carson) that begin or sit inside an unfamiliar name or brand, often a fabricated or obscure one, while the strongest negative cases are word-initial or quantity tokens (Long, power, yards, runs) in sports/strength contexts, which predict a compound or measure follow-up. The negative pole is far larger in magnitude, so the neuron mainly acts as a suppressor when a common word like "power" or "long" starts a compound (powerlifting, Longhorn) or ends a quantity.

LABEL: Positive on name fragments inside rare proper nouns; strongly negative on "power"/"long"/"yards

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on a modifier/adjective token that sits before a noun and predicts what comes next. The positive pole covers evaluative, intensifying or stylistic adjectives (luxury, best, enterprise, catastrophic, informed, perfect) that lead into a flexible open class of nouns. The negative pole covers classifying modifiers (physical, mental, health, legal, motor, immune, sensory) that form tight compound terms, so the next word is nearly fixed (health, activity, system, therapy).

LABEL: Pre-noun modifier tokens: positive for evaluative/intensifying adjectives with open continuations; negative for categorical domain adjectives that predict a fixed compound noun.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on mid-phrase tokens where the word is a modifier or fragment whose meaning depends on the next token (e.g. "automatic" refunds, "issued_by", "direct debit", "private" information, "stuck" refunds), predicting a specific completion in a noun phrase or identifier. The negative pole fires on similar mid-phrase tokens in generic tutorial or instructional text (the "Animated" API, "use" a format specifier, "lazy" loading), where the next token is a highly predictable technical term. So it tracks incomplete modifier or identifier tokens, with sign likely separating the context type: support/ticket/refund-style records versus programming and how-to explanations.

LABEL: Mid-phrase modifier/fragment tokens awaiting a noun or identifier; positive in refund/ticket/finance-record contexts, negative in coding tutorials and how-to inst

ANALYSIS: The negative pole fires overwhelmingly on the "function" token right after "<tool_call>⏎<", where the next token is a tool name like "=get_account_record" (the token after "function" is nearly determined). The positive pole fires on connective/continuation tokens like commas, "and", "the", "also", and colons in lists, where the next word is a fresh content word (especially in recipes, lists, ingredients). Both poles occur at a position where the model is about to emit a specific, highly constrained token: a rigid template slot at the negative end, and an open content-noun/ingredient slot after a function word at the positive end.

LABEL: Negative: the "function" token opening a tool-call template, predicting a tool name; positive: connectives and list punctuation (",", "and", "the", ":") mid-list, predicting a content word.

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on a word-initial or mid-compound fragment where the model is mid-word or mid-phrase, with the next token still pending. Positive cases are mostly adjectives/modifiers that precede a noun ("plain", "integer", "artificial", "rapid", "hazard-ous"), while negative cases are mostly nouns or noun-like heads, often the first piece of a compound ("work|books", "trap|door", "stay|cation", "support"), plus verbs/particles that end a clause. So the neuron seems to separate "a descriptor or qualifier that expects a head noun to follow" (positive) from "a head noun, compound stem, or completed item" (negative).

LABEL: Positive on adjective/qualifier tokens awaiting a following noun ("plain", "integer", "artificial"); negative on noun/compound-stem tokens ("work", "trap", "support") that already name

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at tokens where the model must decide whether the current text continues in the same unit (mid-word, mid-number, mid-name, sentence) or pivots to a structural boundary, with the formatting/tool-call transition after "assistant
" or "

" being a common spot. Positive activations land on newline/paragraph breaks that precede a tool call or a shift to a new section, and on tokens like "the", ":", or a number digit whose continuation is highly constrained. Negative activations land on mid-word or mid-name subword pieces (e.g. "Stink 18«2»", "dimethyl-orbit«ane»") and on boundaries right before a repeated tool call, so the neuron appears to track "what kind of token comes next" by pushing up for one continuation class and down for another.

LABEL: Predicts the next-token class at a boundary: positive for break/newline before a tool call or new

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at tokens where the text is mapping one string onto a transformed or corrected version (abbreviation lists, renames like `Order Date` → `order_date`, typo fixes, symbol substitutions), predicting that a replacement or equivalent token will follow. Positive activation sits on list bullets, arrows, "for"/"be"/"from" in "typo for X" or "symbol for X", and quote openers, which anticipate a transformed variant. The negative pole sits on similar structural tokens (parentheses, commas, quote closers) in explanatory or conversational contexts where no string-to-string mapping is expected, and it is much weaker.

LABEL: Predicts an upcoming substitute or transformed form of a word or string, as in abbreviation, rename, typo-correction or symbol mappings; weakly negative on ordinary punctuation elsewhere.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at structural and transitional tokens: chat-template markers (<|im_end|>, "assistant"), tool-call XML delimiters and newlines, closing punctuation, and the "I" of refusal-style openings ("I do not have access"). The negative pole fires at similar structural spots (newlines between tool parameters, <|im_start|>, mid-word and number fragments, hyphens, apostrophes) but also at tokens inside multi-token words or numbers where the next token is a strongly constrained continuation. Overall it seems to encode a next-token-prediction mode, positive for places where a new segment or specific formulaic continuation begins and negative where the continuation is a mid-word/mid-phrase completion, with no clean semantic topic.

LABEL: Fires on boundary/delimiter tokens (turn ends, tool-call tags, refusal-opening "I") positively, and on

ANALYSIS: Both poles fire on function words or word fragments at points where the next token is highly constrained. The positive pole is dominated by "please" after "Can you" in user requests, plus verbs, adverbs and connectors ("using", "above", "includes") that open a continuation. The negative pole covers "to" in "generate the response to…", "Could" or "you" at the start of a user question, and mid-word fragments of names or garbled spam text.

LABEL: Function-word and mid-token positions where the next token is strongly predictable: positive on "please"/"using"/"above" after "Can you", negative on "to"/"Could you" template slots and name fragments.

ANALYSIS: The strongest positive firings are in the MeSH/medical subject-headings and hashtag/social-media contexts, on tokens inside or just before a label-like term (a heading, acronym fragment, "#", opening quote, "such as", "to"), where a category or keyword is about to be named. The negative pole fires on tokens in technical or compound word pieces and sentence-opening "The" or "assistant" tokens, where the continuation is a concrete specific completion (rack, ort, ide) rather than a category label. So it appears to track whether the next token is predicted to be an indexing/tagging-type term (subject heading, hashtag, keyword) versus a specific concrete completion of a word or phrase.

LABEL: Positive on tokens anticipating a category/keyword/tag term (MeSH headings, hashtags, "such as", "relevant"); negative on word-piece or sentence-start tokens predic

ANALYSIS: The marked token is almost always a subject/pronoun/connective sitting right before a modal or auxiliary verb slot. The neuron predicts which one: the positive pole precedes "do not / will / would / need / if you'd like / is easily", and the negative pole strongly precedes "can / could / cannot" (ability or permission modals). It is essentially a modal-verb predictor, with "can/could" on the negative side and other auxiliaries (do, will, would, need) on the positive side.

LABEL: Predicts the upcoming auxiliary verb: strongly negative when "can/could/cannot" comes next after a subject (e.g. "I can"), positive when "do/will/would/need/if" follows.

ANALYSIS: The neuron tracks the assistant's position relative to taking an action in agentic and chat turns: positive values fall where the assistant is reporting or summarizing a change already made, or acknowledging what it found, so the work is described rather than about to be done. Strongly negative values fall at the point just before the next step happens, such as the token right after an assistant turn begins, at the end of "Sure!/Certainly!" openers, or at colons and clause ends that lead into a tool call or the updated content. So it separates "narrating or recapping completed work" from "about to emit the action or deliverable."

LABEL: Positive on retrospective summaries of completed fixes and findings; negative at turn-start openers and transition tokens right before a tool call or the requested content.

ANALYSIS: Positive activations land on repeated or enumerated items just before a sentence/paragraph boundary or narrative pivot (e.g. the final "3" in "3+3+3+1", "As they..." story openers), and on chat-template/tool-call structural tokens. Negative activations land on the first digit of a number or date ("2" in 24, 2023, HP-2…) and on newline/tag tokens beginning a tool_response or tool_call. Both poles involve predicting what comes next at a structural seam, with positive favoring continuation of a repeating or narrative pattern and negative favoring the start of a fresh numeric or structured field.

LABEL: Tracks structural-seam positions: positive on repeated list items and prose-transition tokens, negative on leading digits of numbers and tool-call/response delimiter tokens.

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on the head noun or word completing a noun phrase in confident, promotional, or encyclopedic text (e.g. "program", "expertise", "space" in "space exploration"), where the continuation is a generic, predictable phrase. The negative pole fires on mid-word fragments of rare names, on "I cannot" refusals, and on the tokens of fictional or uncertain entities, where the model is hedging or the next token is uncertain. So the neuron seems to track how confidently and fluently the text is asserting familiar facts versus being at an uncertain, name-fragment, or refusal point.

LABEL: Positive on completed head nouns in confident, familiar promotional or factual prose; negative on mid-word name fragments, refusals, and fictional or hedged entities.

ANALYSIS: Activations are small and diffuse, on tokens where the next word is highly constrained or a continuation is expected. The positive pole fires at sentence/response openers and punctuation (e.g. after "instruction:", "Oh, wow", "As an AI") and at mid-word fragments. The negative pole fires at mid-phrase tokens inside a fixed expression or list item ("in terms of", "three times the", "Edit"/"Modify" buttons, padded table whitespace), where the continuation is nearly determined.

LABEL: Positive at response/sentence openers where the next word is open-ended; negative mid-phrase inside fixed collocations, lists or formatted structures where the continuation is predetermined.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on the word completing a loss/depletion/deprivation construction — the object of a verb like stealing, stripping, slipping, losing, or blocking ("stealing American «jobs»", "hours «slip»", "losing «valuable» time"). The positive pole is the token right at that point of being taken, drained, or removed from someone; the negative pole fires on similar loss/threat/fragility words (loss of, losing control, threat, fragility) but more often on the head noun or function word of an abstract "loss of X" frame in the middle of a phrase. Both poles track the same semantic frame of something being lost, at-risk, or fragile, differing in the token's role.

LABEL: Tracks tokens inside loss/theft/depletion/fragility phrases: positive on the thing being taken or slipping away, negative on the "loss of/losing/threat" framing words.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at the first word right after a directive or condition that sets up a requirement ("ensure", "write", "throw new Error(", "if…"), and the sign depends on whether that word is a modifier/adjective/quantifier or a noun-phrase head. Positive: modifiers and openers like "No", "Invalid", "effective", "clean", "font", "practical", "Clear" that begin a descriptive or error-handling phrase. Negative: determiners and subject nouns ("the", "your", "program", "essay", "quotes", "images") that start a requirement clause, plus "assistant" at turn starts, i.e. where a noun-phrase subject is being named and its predicate is still pending.

LABEL: Distinguishes a requirement clause's opening modifier or negation (positive) from its subject noun or determiner (negative), i.e. whether the next word is a noun or a predicate.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on tokens where "record"/"database"-type structure is about to appear or has just been invoked: positive on the first characters of tabular/CSV records and "record" nouns, negative on tokens inside or right before database/field/tool-call parameters like "of", "SH" (MeSH), "activ(erecord)", "function", and newline after get_batch. The extreme values (+23.9 / -23.9) look like a single large-magnitude token whose sign depends on whether the context is a data row/record versus the entity or query that retrieves one. In effect it tracks the record-versus-database/schema boundary, with weaker activations on mid-phrase tokens inside "record" and "database" phrases.

LABEL: Marks tokens tied to data records/databases: positive on record rows and "record" words, negative on database/query terms, tool-call scaffolding, and phrase-internal tokens like "of"/

ANALYSIS: Activations fall on mid-word or mid-phrase fragments and structural boundary tokens (word-piece splits like "Aberc|rom|bie", "gas|light|ing", chat-template newlines/<|im_end|>, "if you'll| excuse"), where the model is still waiting for the continuation. The positive pole favors fragments where the next piece is highly predictable/forced (Abercrombie, "here's the tea", "new hashset", "Please don't tell anyone"), while the negative pole fires on similar boundary points, especially the "assistant" role token and set phrases like "I've had enough of", where the next content is open-ended or about to begin a response. So it seems to track token-boundary position within multi-token units and chat-turn scaffolding rather than semantic content.

LABEL: Fires on incomplete word fragments and chat-template boundary tokens; positive when the continuation is near-deter

ANALYSIS: The positive pole fires on the final noun of a "X and Y" coordination when that noun is a countable quantity or nutrient/stat category (touchdowns after "yards and", protein/fiber/sugar after "high in X and"). It predicts a stat-line or nutrition list continuation. The negative pole is weak, fires on mid-word fragments and proper-noun pieces (Phos-gene, Saudi, Gam-ble), where the token is an incomplete name or term.

LABEL: Fires strongly on "touchdowns" (and nutrient nouns like protein/fiber) completing a "yards and N X" or "high in X and Y" pair; weakly negative on mid-word name fragments.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires on tokens that sit at a junction where the next token is a variable reference, an identifier, or a quoted/reported continuation: positive on the connector (" +", " and", "says", closing quote/comma) and strongly negative on the identifier fragment itself (the "Title" in eventTitle, "software" in $softwareName) or the closing quote of a string. In other words it separates "operator/connector awaiting an operand" from "operand or string-end already completed", especially in concatenation, attribution, and print/console calls. The two poles are the two sides of a junction, one before a continuation and the other after a completed name or quoted unit.

LABEL: Positive on connector tokens (+, and, says, console., closing quote) awaiting an operand or continuation; negative on the completed identifier/name pieces and string-ending quotes.

ANALYSIS: The neuron fires at formatting/structural boundary tokens, where the next token begins a new content unit. Positive: the newline right after an empty `</think>` or an assistant/user turn marker (where a refusal or "I'll start by…" begins), and opening parentheses or bold markers after a list heading. Negative: the opening `**` of a bolded label, or mid-word fragments (Full|Calendar, v|Card, Clean|Green, hyphens in ranges) where the next token completes the compound unit.

LABEL: Positive on turn-start newlines/parentheses opening a new response or clause; negative on bold-label openers and mid-word compound fragments needing a completion.

ANALYSIS: The largest activations in both directions, roughly ±20 to ±47, land on structural or boundary tokens (a possessive "'s", newline, "-", "." in an IP address, a role token after <|im_end|>) where the model is at a junction and a lot of upcoming content rides on a single token. The neuron looks like a very-high-magnitude, sparse feature that fires at such junctions, with its sign flipping depending on context: positive in conversational, fiction and list text, negative in code/tool-call, path and formatting contexts. The small activations (a few units either way) on ordinary function words ("the", "with", "her") are weak background noise on the same dimension.

LABEL: Rare huge-magnitude spikes on structural junction tokens (newlines, punctuation, possessives, role tags), positive in prose/fiction/list contexts and negative in code/tool-call contexts.
